title: The Quiet Qualities
subject: English
unit: Spring 2: Julius Caesar (Shakespeare): leadership, persuasion and responsibility
source: Written for english/y8 lesson 30 ('The Quiet Qualities' (teacher-written opinion article, pupil PDF))
intro: Lesson 30: Non-fiction: what makes a great leader?. Read the whole text, then annotate it: underline the writer's methods and note their effect in the margin.

passage.title: The Quiet Qualities
paras: We often confuse leaders with the loudest people in the room. Yet history suggests that great leaders share three quieter qualities. The first is integrity: people follow those whose words and actions match. The second is humility: a leader who listens makes fewer fatal mistakes. The third is accountability: the best leaders accept that power must answer to someone.
Consider the captain who is last to leave a sinking ship. Nobody elected her for her speeches. They trust her because she puts the crew first.

Charisma has its uses. A confident voice can calm a frightened crowd, and a stirring speech can make people brave. But charisma without integrity is dangerous. History is full of persuasive speakers who led their followers into disaster, because nobody dared to ask whether the words were true.

Humility is easy to mistake for weakness. It is not. A humble leader still decides; she simply decides after she has heard the people who will be affected. In a school, that might be the head teacher who asks pupils why a rule is not working before changing it. In a business, it is the manager who admits a mistake in front of the team.
Accountability may be the hardest quality of all, because it means accepting that you can be questioned, corrected and even removed. Yet it is also what makes power safe.

So the next time you choose a team captain or vote for a class representative, listen past the loudest voice. Ask instead: Do their actions match their words? Do they listen? Will they answer for what they do? The quiet qualities, in the end, are the ones that last.

questions.q: What is the writer's main viewpoint?
questions.a: Great leaders are defined by integrity, humility and accountability, not loudness.

questions.q: Find two methods the writer uses and explain the effect of each.
questions.a: The rule of three; the anecdote of the captain; contrast with charisma; direct address in the final questions.

questions.q: How does the final paragraph end the argument?
questions.a: With three questions to the reader and a short memorable final sentence.

questions.q: Retrieve the three qualities and give a one-line definition of each.
questions.a: Integrity (words match actions); humility (listens); accountability (power answers to someone).

questions.q: What is the effect of the short final sentence?
questions.a: It is blunt and memorable, stressing that trust comes from putting others first.

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, explain how the writer persuades the reader about leadership, using two methods. Starter: 'The writer argues that great leaders...'
questions.a: Viewpoint plus two methods (e.g. rule of three, anecdote) with effects and evidence.

questions.q: Extend: which quality does Caesar most lack so far? Use the play.
questions.a: Humility: he speaks of himself in the third person and seems to rise above others.

questions.q: Stretch: add a fourth quality the writer missed and justify it.
questions.a: For example: justice, because a leader must treat people fairly.

questions.q: Why does the writer use the captain anecdote?
options: To tell a true news story
To prove captains are always women
To make an abstract quality concrete and memorable
questions.a: C) To make an abstract quality concrete and memorable. An anecdote humanises the argument; the other options misread its purpose.
B) not thinking you are better than others
options: not thinking you are better than others

questions.q: Answer the ponder in one sentence, using a word from today.
questions.a: For example: an honest leader, because integrity builds trust that cleverness alone cannot.
